name: Orlistat
lead: Orlistat is a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor used with a reduced-calorie diet for weight loss in adults. It is sold by prescription as Xenical (120 mg capsules) and over the counter as Alli (60 mg capsules), and it works inside the gut rather than being absorbed into the bloodstream [1][7][14]. Reviews describe it as one of five or so drugs available for long-term obesity treatment in the US, with weight loss smaller than that of newer injectable drugs [3][5][4].

Trials such as the 1998 European multicentre study and a 2-year US trial found greater weight loss on orlistat than placebo [8][10]. Grokipedia describes an average extra loss of about 2 to 3 kg over 6 to 12 months [1]. The most commonly reported side effects are gastrointestinal, including oily spotting and urgency, reported in more than 25% of patients in one review [3].

In bodybuilding and fat-loss forums such as T Nation, orlistat is discussed as a fat blocker and was described in 2006 as a possible replacement for ephedrine [16][17]. Some posters report diarrhea and little benefit [15][19].

paras: The Alli label states it is for weight loss in overweight adults aged 18 and older when used with a reduced-calorie, low-fat diet [14]. Grokipedia reports prescription Xenical is indicated for BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with comorbidities, and for adolescents aged 12 to 16 [1]. Studies have also examined its effect on liver fat in obese patients with fatty liver disease, on diabetes prevention, and on cholesterol [6][9][7].

Its appearance relevance is limited to modest fat loss. Users in forums discuss it as a fat-absorption blocker during diets and cutting phases, and several posters question whether it suits people who already restrict dietary fat [21][22].

A randomized placebo-controlled trial in obese patients (European Multicentre Orlistat Study Group, 1998) tested weight loss and prevention of regain [8]. A 2-year randomized trial in the US examined weight control and risk factors [10]. The 4-year XENDOS trial studied orlistat as an adjunct to lifestyle change for preventing type 2 diabetes in obese subjects [9]. Earlier reviews noted reductions in total and LDL cholesterol over up to two years [7].

Network meta-analyses of weight-loss drugs place orlistat among the less effective options relative to semaglutide and tirzepatide [2][4]. A 2023 randomized trial in Asian adults with obesity and fatty liver compared orlistat with a diet [6]. Other registered studies include trials on uric acid, polycystic ovary syndrome and maintenance after weight loss [11][12][13].

Reviews report oily fecal spotting, urgency and other gastrointestinal effects in more than 25% of patients [3]. Grokipedia adds flatulence and steatorrhea, with dose dependence, and notes that fat-soluble vitamin absorption can be affected, so a multivitamin is advised [1].

The OTC label contains warnings: do not use after organ transplant, with cyclosporine, in people with food-absorption problems, or if allergic to ingredients; ask a doctor if there is a history of gallbladder problems, kidney stones or pancreatitis [14].

Orlistat binds covalently to gastric and pancreatic lipases in the gut, preventing them from breaking down dietary triglycerides, so that a fraction of fat, described by Grokipedia as 25 to 30%, passes into stool [1][7]. Systemic absorption is minimal [1].

Roche developed orlistat from lipstatin, a compound produced by the bacterium Streptomyces toxytricini [1]. Xenical was approved in the US in April 1999 and the lower-dose Alli received OTC approval in 2007, according to Grokipedia [1]. A 2006 T Nation thread predicted OTC orlistat might be sold in mass market stores [17].

Forum discussions on T Nation from 2002 to 2017 include questions about combining orlistat with other drugs, its place in contest preparation stacks, and reports of diarrhea [20][21][23][15]. One poster argued bodybuilders already have strict diets and have less use for it [22].

lore.intro: Orlistat is mentioned in bodybuilding and fat-loss forums as an inexpensive fat blocker with unpleasant digestive effects [15][18].

claims.claim: Orlistat blocks fat absorption so it helps cutting
claims.believers: Posters describe it as a fat-absorption blocker used in diet and contest-prep contexts [21][18].
claims.experts: Randomized trials found greater weight loss than placebo, with an extra 2 to 3 kg reported over 6 to 12 months [10][1].

claims.claim: Orlistat is ineffective for people already on a low-fat diet
claims.believers: A poster states bodybuilders with strict diets have little reason to use it, and another said three months did not help someone [22][19].
claims.experts: The label and trials pair it with a reduced-calorie, low-fat diet; fat-containing meals trigger the digestive effects [14][1].

claims.claim: Orlistat is a safe replacement for banned stimulants
claims.believers: A 2006 thread lists it as a safer alternative to ephedra products [16].
claims.experts: Its documented effects are gastrointestinal, with label warnings about drug interactions and some health conditions [3][14].

card.summary: OTC and Rx fat-absorption blocker that adds a few kilos of weight loss over placebo at the price of oily stools.
card.note: GI side effects common; label warns against use with cyclosporine and after organ transplant.

quick.overview:
Orlistat is a capsule taken with meals that blocks the enzymes that digest dietary fat. The 60 mg Alli is sold over the counter; the 120 mg Xenical needs a prescription.

Trials show weight loss greater than placebo, but modest compared with newer injectable drugs; about 2 to 3 kg extra over 6 to 12 months is cited.
quick.mechanism: Orlistat inhibits lipase enzymes in the stomach and pancreas, so some of the fat in a meal is not absorbed and leaves in the stool. Very little enters the bloodstream.
quick.risks: Oily spotting, urgency, gas and loose stools are common, especially with fatty meals. It can reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, and the label warns against use after organ transplant or with cyclosporine.
